steps.surface: Chat view — a reply that used several different kinds of tools in one step
steps.path: Today this line reads: "3 Tools (Bash, Write, Grep) — all complete" — internal names, not plain words
steps.headline: When several DIFFERENT kinds of things happened, how many should the sentence name before folding the rest into a count?

options.label: Name the first 2, fold the rest into a count you can click open (recommended)
options.summary: Proposal: "Created a file and ran a command (+1 more)". Clicking the line (it already opens today) shows every step by name, so nothing is hidden, just shortened. Pro: stays short and easy to scan no matter how busy the step was. Con: on a busy step (5-6 different kinds of things) you see 2 named and have to click for the rest.
options.cost: A short combining rule, plus reusing the click-to-expand the line already has.

options.label: Name every kind of thing that happened, never fold anything
options.summary: "Created a file, ran a command, searched the web and read a file" — nothing hidden. Pro: everything visible without clicking. Con: on a busy step the line gets long and wraps, which works against the whole point of making this easier to read at a glance.
options.cost: No cutoff logic, but the line's length becomes unpredictable.

options.label: Name only 1 kind of thing, fold everything else into a count
options.summary: "Created a file (+3 more)". Pro: shortest possible line. Con: throws away most of the "what did it actually do" information this request is asking for — close to as uninformative as today's version.

steps.surface: Chat view — a step that ran the same kind of thing more than once (e.g. three commands)
steps.path: The app already writes "Invoked 2 skills: brainstorming and writing-plans" for repeated skills — this asks whether every tool type should work the same way
steps.headline: When the same kind of thing happens more than once, should the sentence say how many?

options.label: Yes, always show the number — "ran 3 commands" (recommended)
options.summary: Matches the wording already shipped for repeated skills. Pro: consistent with what's already in the app, and the number is often the useful part — "read 8 files" tells you it searched broadly, "ran 3 commands" tells you it did more than a quick check. Con: none seen.
options.cost: None beyond what's already built for the skills case.

options.label: Never show the number — always just "ran commands"
options.summary: Shortest, but one command and ten commands read exactly the same, which hides how much actually happened.
options.cost: Simpler, but throws away real information.

options.label: Only show the number at 3 or more; say just "ran a command" / "ran commands" below that
options.summary: A middle ground. Con: one more rule to remember, and it wouldn't match the skills wording, which always shows the number.
options.cost: An extra rule, and an inconsistency with the skills line.

steps.surface: Chat view — a step where one thing failed, or is waiting on your approval, among others that finished fine
steps.path: Today's line already ends with "— 1 failed" or "— waiting on you" (the waiting-on-you part is highlighted in color) — this only asks whether that stays as-is under the new wording
steps.headline: How should a failure, or something waiting on your approval, show up in the new plain-language line?

options.label: Keep today's ending exactly, just reworded in plain words (recommended)
options.summary: "Created a file and ran a command — 1 failed" / "...— waiting on you" (still color-highlighted). Pro: reuses a part of today's line that already works well and is proven; nothing new to design. Con: none seen.
options.cost: None — this part of the code is unchanged.

options.label: Weave the failure into the sentence itself — "Tried to run a command, but it failed"
options.summary: Reads more conversationally for exactly one failure, but gets wordy and hard to write a clean rule for once several different things are mixed together in one step.
options.cost: New sentence-building rules for every combination of success/failure.

options.label: Don't mention it in the summary line at all — only show it once you click to expand
options.summary: Shortest line, but hides the one thing — a failure, or something that needs your yes/no — most worth noticing at a glance. Works against the purpose of this line.
options.cost: Least code, but a real risk of a missed approval or failure.

steps.surface: Chat view — a step that used an outside connection (Gmail, Google Calendar, a community plugin) rather than one of the app's built-in tools
steps.path: The built-in tools (running a command, reading/writing a file, searching, etc.) each already have a plain-word phrase; outside connections don't yet
steps.headline: For an outside connection, should the sentence name the service, or stay generic?

options.label: Name the service when the app already knows its friendly name — "checked Gmail" (recommended)
options.summary: Most outside connections already show a friendly name elsewhere in the app (Gmail, Google Calendar, Canva). Reuse that name here; fall back to a generic "used a tool" only for the rare one with no friendly name on file. Pro: as specific as possible for free, since the name already exists somewhere in the app. Con: none seen.
options.cost: Reuses a name lookup the app already has for these connections.

options.label: Always say "used a tool", no matter which service
options.summary: Simpler, but throws away information the app already has — you'd see "used a tool" instead of "checked Gmail" even when it's known exactly what happened.
options.cost: Simplest, but a step backward from how specific the built-in tools already read.

steps.surface: Chat view — a step where some things are still running while others already finished, and one of the finished ones failed
steps.path: Your own example was "Creating a file, editing an image, running commands (+3 completed)" — this asks what happens when one of those 3 already-finished things failed
steps.headline: If something already finished has failed while other things are still running, should the count split it out right away?

options.label: Yes — split it out immediately, e.g. "(+2 completed, 1 failed)" (recommended)
options.summary: Keeps the most urgent fact — a failure — visible the moment it happens, instead of waiting for the whole step to finish. Pro: you never have to wait to notice a problem. Con: the line is a little longer when there's a mix.
options.cost: Combines two counts the app already tracks separately today.

options.label: No — keep one combined "completed" count until everything finishes, e.g. "(+3 completed)"
options.summary: Shorter while things are still running, but a failure could sit unnoticed inside that "completed" count until the whole step wraps up and the line updates.
options.cost: Simplest, but can hide a failure that already happened.
